title: Don't give to get more
hook: do not give expecting to get more (74:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Muddaththir, and your line, arise. Did you get up for something you wanted to hide from? Two verses further into al-Muddaththir, a fifth command. Day six hundred fifty-six.

You know the gift with a string on it. The favor that comes back up in an argument six months later: after everything I did for you. The wedding present chosen to impress. The donation made mostly for the plaque. The help offered so that, one day, help will be owed. Most giving has a little ledger behind it, even when we don't admit it. Just after the call to arise, al-Muddaththir gives the Prophet a short instruction that goes straight at that ledger.

Verse six is four words in Arabic: wa la tamnun tastakthir. Don't give, seeking more. Tamnun comes from mann, which carries two ideas: to bestow a favor, and to remind someone of it, to hold it over them. Tastakthir means to seek more, or to count something as a lot. And the commentators read the verse in more than one way. One early reading, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, is the plainest: don't give a gift so that you'll get a bigger one back. Another reading: don't consider what you've done as much. Don't stand before your Lord counting your good deeds as if they were a favor to Him. A third: don't remind people of the good you've done for them. Many commentators say the verse holds all of these. They're the same habit, seen from different sides: keeping score. The Qur'an returns to this in surah al-Baqarah, where it says: don't cancel your charity with reminders and hurt. A gift held over someone isn't really a gift anymore; it's a loan with interest. And look at what comes right after, verse seven: for your Lord, be patient. The giving and the patience are a pair. If you give without expecting a return, you'll need patience, because sometimes nothing comes back. No thanks, no favor, no recognition. The verse doesn't promise you'll be repaid by people. It removes the repayment from the transaction entirely. You give, and then you let it go, and you wait, if you wait at all, on Someone else.

The practice: give with nothing in return. Sit, and think of someone you could give something to today. Time, a meal, a ride, a coin, a kind word. Then check for a string. Do I want thanks? Credit? A favor later? Don't scold yourself if you find one; almost everyone does. Just notice it, and picture cutting it. Picture giving, and then not mentioning it to anyone, ever. The bell holds the time.
Tamnun tastakthir. In 74:6, don't give seeking more: don't hold a favor over anyone, and don't count your good as much. Today's word.
Your line: give, don't count. Today, give one thing quietly, and then leave it out of every conversation, including the one in your head. Day six hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to give charity without reminding the recipient of it or expecting return, citing 74:6 and 2:264; many give secretly so that, as a hadith says, the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.

match.prompt: don't give to get more — tap the pairs.
pairs: a favor, or holding it over someone
don't give to get a bigger gift

myth: commentators read 74:6 in only one way
readings include: don't give to get more, don't count your deeds, don't remind.
al-Baqarah says reminders and hurt cancel charity
a gift held over someone stops being a gift.
the verse promises that people will repay you
it removes repayment from the giving; verse seven asks for patience.

fork.setup: a friend you helped last year is arguing with you. you're tempted to say: after everything I did for you. what does 74:6 point to?
options: don't hold the favor over them.
fork.reveal: one reading of wa la tamnun is exactly this: don't remind people of what you gave, and don't count it as much.

original.note: Arabic, 74:6: don't give (or remind of a favor) seeking more.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be greedy when you give.
what it means: give without a ledger: not for a bigger return, not counting your deeds, not holding it over anyone.
what a scholar hears: mann means both bestowing and reminding of a favor; Ibn 'Abbas's reading is the gift for a larger gift, and 2:264 echoes it.

notes: 74:6 paraphrased, not quoted; Pickthall's exact wording was not certain.
The readings of 74:6 (Ibn 'Abbas: don't give to receive more; don't count your deeds as much; don't remind of a favor) follow classical tafsir such as at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir; confirm attributions.
Bukhari 1423 (the seven under Allah's shade, including secret charity) cited from memory in howItsDone; confirm.
